title: Longest Word in Dictionary
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every prefix of every word versus sorting and verifying only the immediate prefix per word.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of strings words, return the longest word that can be built one character at a time by other words in words, meaning every prefix of that word (of every length) must also exist in words. If there are multiple such longest words, return the lexicographically smallest one; if none qualify, return an empty string.

blocks.text: A word qualifies only if ALL of its prefixes (length 1, 2, 3, ..., full length) are also present in words. Sorting words lexicographically means any word's (length-1) prefix, if present at all, will have been processed BEFORE the word itself, so checking just that immediate prefix (rather than all prefixes from scratch) suffices, as long as a "confirmed buildable" set is maintained.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building LEGO Towers Where Each New Brick Requires the Shorter Tower to Already Be Confirmed Stable
blocks.text: Picture building word-towers one letter at a time, where adding a new letter is only allowed if the tower one letter shorter has ALREADY been confirmed as buildable itself. Processing potential towers from shortest to longest, and checking only the immediately preceding, one-shorter tower, correctly builds up which towers are ultimately valid.

blocks.caption: Sorting ensures a word's immediate prefix is processed first; checking just that prefix against a confirmed set suffices

blocks.text: Result: "world". Every prefix of "world" (w, wo, wor, worl) is present in words.

Before checking every prefix of every word from scratch, notice that sorting words lexicographically guarantees a word's immediate (length-1) prefix, IF it is buildable, will already have been confirmed in an earlier iteration, so only that single immediate prefix needs checking, not the full chain.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A word is buildable if and only if its immediate prefix (itself one character shorter) is ALSO buildable, recursively down to the empty string (trivially buildable).

Observation 2: Sorting words lexicographically ensures that if a word's immediate prefix exists in the list at all, it will be processed BEFORE the word itself (since it is lexicographically smaller, being a prefix).

Observation 3: Maintaining a "confirmed buildable" set, initialized with the empty string, lets each word be checked in O(1) against just its immediate prefix, rather than re-verifying the entire chain.

Observation 4: If a word's immediate prefix is confirmed, the word itself becomes confirmed too, and its length is compared against the current longest answer.

This leads to sorting words, then a single pass: for each word, check if its immediate prefix is in the confirmed set; if so, add the word to the set and update the answer if it is longer (or tied but lexicographically smaller, handled naturally by sort order).
For each word, check whether every one of its prefixes exists in the words list, tracking the longest word that fully qualifies.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every prefix of every word directly implements the definition, guaranteed correct.
This costs O(n times L squared) (L being max word length), re-verifying the same prefixes repeatedly across different words.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times L squared).
Space: O(n times L) for the word set.
Limitation: sorting first lets each word be checked in O(1) against just its immediate prefix, achieving O(n log n) total instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Sort words lexicographically. Maintain a "confirmed buildable" set, starting with just the empty string. For each word in sorted order, check if its immediate (length-1) prefix is already in this set; if so, the word itself becomes confirmed, added to the set, and compared against the current best answer.

Sort words. For each word, check if word[:-1] is in the confirmed set; if so, add word to the set and update the best answer if longer (sorting handles the lexicographic tie-break naturally, since shorter/equal-length ties are processed in lexicographic order).

Sorting guarantees that any word's immediate prefix, if it exists in words at all, is processed strictly before the word itself (since it is lexicographically smaller). This means checking whether that immediate prefix has ALREADY been confirmed buildable (transitively verifying its own full prefix chain, already done in earlier iterations) is exactly equivalent to checking the word's entire prefix chain, but in O(1) rather than re-verifying it from scratch.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(n times L) for the confirmed set.

blocks.text: Longest Word in Dictionary is a clean example of sorting to convert a "verify the entire chain" problem into a "verify just the immediate predecessor" problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "every prefix must also be present in the list", think: sort first, then verify only the immediate prefix against a running confirmed set.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Checking every prefix of every word costs O(n times L squared) time; sorting and checking only the immediate prefix costs O(n log n) time, both using O(n times L) space.

items: Pattern: sort first to guarantee immediate prefixes are processed before their extensions, then verify in O(1) per word.
Core Idea: maintain a confirmed-buildable set (seeded with the empty string); a word qualifies iff its immediate prefix is already confirmed.
Time: O(n times L squared) for checking every prefix, O(n log n) for the sort-based approach.
Most Important Observation: sorting converts "verify the full prefix chain" into "verify just the immediate predecessor," since that predecessor's own chain was already verified earlier.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible problem rewarding recognition of the sort-based simplification.
One line memory trick: sort words; a word qualifies iff its immediate prefix is already confirmed.
